abstract: While the cellular heat-shock response has been a paradigm for studying the impact of thermal stress on RNA metabolism and gene expression, the genome-wide response to thermal stress and its connection to physiological stress resistance remain largely unexplored. Here, we address this issue using an array-based exon expression analysis to interrogate the transcriptome in recently established Drosophila melanogaster stocks during severe thermal stress and recovery. We first demonstrated the efficacy of exon-level analyses to reveal a level of thermally induced transcriptome complexity extending well beyond gene-level analyses. Next, we showed that the upper range of both the cellular and physiological thermal stress response profoundly affected message expression and processing in D. melanogaster, limiting expression to a small subset of transcripts, many that share features of known rapidly responding stress genes. As predicted from cellular heat-shock research, constitutive splicing was blocked in a set of novel genes; we did not detect changes to alternative splicing during heat stress, but rather induction of intronless isoforms of known heat-responsive genes. We observed transcriptome plasticity in the form of differential isoform expression during recovery from heat shock, mediated by multiple mechanisms including alternative transcription and alternative splicing. This affected genes involved in DNA regulation, immune response, and thermotolerance. These patterns highlight the complex nature of innate transcriptome responses under stress and potential for adaptive shifts through plasticity and evolved genetic responses at different hierarchical levels.
title: New Levels of Transcriptome Complexity at Upper Thermal Limits in Wild Drosophila Revealed by Exon Expression Analysis
author: Marina Telonis-Scott; Belinda van Heerwaarden; Travis K. Johnson; Ary A. Hoffmann; Carla M. Sgrò
keywords: Drosophila; heat stress; splicing; thermal extremes; transcription

abstract: Cold tolerance is a key determinant of insect distribution and abundance, and thermal acclimation can strongly influence organismal stress tolerance phenotypes, particularly in small ectotherms like Drosophila. However, there is limited understanding of the molecular and biochemical mechanisms that confer such impressive plasticity. Here, we use high-throughput mRNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to compare the transcriptomes and metabolomes of D. melanogaster acclimated as adults to warm (rearing) (21.5 °C) or cold conditions (6 °C). Cold acclimation improved cold tolerance and led to extensive biological reorganization: almost one third of the transcriptome and nearly half of the metabolome were differentially regulated. There was overlap in the metabolic pathways identified via transcriptomics and metabolomics, with proline and glutathione metabolism being the most strongly-supported metabolic pathways associated with increased cold tolerance. We discuss several new targets in the study of insect cold tolerance, but many previously identified candidate genes and pathways were also identified in the present study.
title: Cold acclimation wholly reorganizes the Drosophila melanogaster transcriptome and metabolome
author: Heath A. MacMillan; Jose M. Knee; Alice B. Dennis; Hiroko Udaka; Katie E. Marshall; Thomas J. S. Merritt; Brent J. Sinclair

abstract: Phenotypic plasticity enables a single genotype to produce multiple phenotypes in response to environmental variation. This study examined rapid parallel regulatory adaptation of Anolis lizards to urban heat islands and found evidence that adaptation was driven largely by reduced or reversed heat-induced plasticity that was maladaptive in urban thermal conditions. Forest lizards showed heat-induced expression changes associated with decreased heat tolerance, whereas urban lizards displayed reduced expression plasticity and more expression change congruent with greater heat tolerance.
title: Selection on adaptive and maladaptive gene expression plasticity during thermal adaptation to urban heat islands
author: Shane C. Campbell-Staton; Jonathan P. Velotta; Kristin M. Winchell

abstract: We studied the evolution of developmental plasticity in populations of Drosophila melanogaster that evolved at either constant or fluctuating temperatures. Genotypes that evolved at a constant 16 °C or 25 °C performed best when raised and tested at that temperature. Genotypes that evolved at fluctuating temperatures performed well at either temperature, but only when raised and tested at the same temperature. The results support predicted specialist-generalist trade-offs, including a loss of plasticity and a benefit of specialization in constant environments.
title: Developmental plasticity evolved according to specialist-generalist trade-offs in experimental populations of Drosophila melanogaster
author: Jacqueline Le Vinh Thuy; John M. VandenBrooks; Michael J. Angilletta Jr
keywords: Drosophila; experimental evolution; performance; plasticity; selection; temperature

abstract: Under current climate change, increasing mean temperatures are accompanied by increasing temperature variability. In an experiment with 11 Arabidopsis thaliana genotypes, the timing but not frequency of temperature stress affected phenology, growth, reproduction and allocation, and genotypes differed substantially in their responses. Trait plasticity was positively related to precipitation variability of origin, suggesting an adaptive role of plasticity.
title: Phenotypic plasticity in response to temperature fluctuations is genetically variable, and relates to climatic variability of origin, in Arabidopsis thaliana
author: J. F. Scheepens; Ying Deng; Oliver Bossdorf
keywords: Adaptation; climatic variability; genotype; heat stress; intraspecific variation; phenotypic plasticity

abstract: Phenotypic plasticity is the ability of a single genotype to produce different phenotypes in response to changing environments. Genome-wide gene expression and four fitness-related phenotypes were assessed in an outbred Drosophila melanogaster population under 20 different environments. Environmentally sensitive transcripts comprised about 15% of expressed transcripts and fell into two broad classes with distinct genetic and functional properties. The results suggest that a restricted environmentally responsive segment of the transcriptome preserves a balance between phenotypic plasticity and environmental canalization.
title: Phenotypic Plasticity of the Drosophila Transcriptome
author: Shanshan Zhou; Terry G. Campbell; Eric A. Stone; Trudy F. C. Mackay; Robert R. H. Anholt

abstract: Embryogenesis is remarkably robust to temperature variability, yet the homeostatic mechanisms that offset thermal effects during early development remain poorly understood. The study measured how acclimation shifts the upper thermal limit and profiled chromatin accessibility and gene expression in Drosophila melanogaster embryos using single-nucleus multiome sequencing. Cool-acclimated embryos showed increased accessibility at Zelda binding motifs and elevated ribosomal and oxidative-phosphorylation gene expression, suggesting coordinated homeostatic regulation across temperature.
title: Single-nucleus multiome sequencing reveals the molecular basis of thermal acclimation in Drosophila melanogaster embryos
author: Thomas S. O'Leary; Emily E. Mikucki; Sumaetee Tangwancharoen; Joseph R. Boyd; Sara Helms Cahan; Seth Frietze; Brent L. Lockwood

abstract: Zymoseptoria tritici causes Septoria tritici blotch on wheat and shows substantial intraspecific variation in virulence. Deep transcriptomic sequencing across an infection time course revealed seven major transcriptional clusters corresponding to distinct infection stages. Major components of the infection transcriptome were conserved between strains, but individual secreted proteins, proteases and cell-wall degrading enzymes showed strongly differentiated transcriptional profiles.
title: Comparative transcriptomic analyses of Zymoseptoria tritici strains show complex lifestyle transitions and intraspecific variability in transcription profiles
author: Javier Palma-Guerrero; Stefano F. F. Torriani; Marcello Zala; Dee Carter; Mikaël Courbot; Jason J. Rudd; Bruce A. McDonald; Daniel Croll
keywords: RNA sequencing; Septoria leaf blotch; Zymoseptoria tritici; comparative transcriptomics; hemibiotroph

abstract: To investigate the molecular basis of temperature stress responses in Zymoseptoria tritici, quantitative trait locus mapping was conducted for colony growth and melanization at 10, 18 and 27 °C in two crosses involving four Swiss parents. Temperature-specific QTL were identified, and candidate regions contained genes involved in heat-shock and MAPK pathways, including an ammonium transporter, Whi1, Ssk2 and Opy2.
title: Mapping genomic regions associated with temperature stress in the wheat pathogen Zymoseptoria tritici
author: Jessica Stapley; Ziming Zhong; Bruce A. McDonald
keywords: Mycosphaerella graminicola; QTL; fungi; heat stress; plant pathogen; quantitative trait loci

abstract: Drosophila melanogaster populations subjected to constant high-temperature and fluctuating-temperature regimes for 80 generations showed extensive transcriptomic and phenotypic adaptation. RNA sequencing identified 1288 and 1152 differentially expressed genes in the two regimes, respectively. Shared and regime-specific pathways were detected, and evolved populations showed increased heat tolerance, accelerated development and prolonged longevity.
title: Experimental evolution-induced transcriptome and phenotype responses of Drosophila melanogaster to novel thermal environments
author: Dau Dayal Aggarwal; Prachi Mishra; Yashvant Patel; Manvender Singh; Vijendra Sharma; Abraham B. Korol; Pawel Michalak
keywords: Genomic adaptation; Physiological assays; Thermal regime-specific patterns; Thermal stress; Transcriptome profiling

abstract: The transcriptome of the fungal wheat pathogen Zymoseptoria tritici was studied after experimental evolution under stable or fluctuating temperature. Temperature regimes had a large effect on transcriptome evolution, with up to 38% of genes differentially expressed between selection regimes. Evolution under fluctuating conditions was repeatable among parallel lineages from the same genotype for about 60% of differentially expressed genes, and fluctuating lines showed a general trend toward increased robustness and loss of phenotypic plasticity.
title: Evolution and Plasticity of the Transcriptome Under Temperature Fluctuations in the Fungal Plant Pathogen Zymoseptoria tritici
author: Arthur J. Jallet; Arnaud Le Rouzic; Anne Genissel
keywords: RNA-seq; adaptive evolution; experimental evolution; fluctuation; gene expression; plasticity; temperature

abstract: The wheat pathogen Zymoseptoria tritici was transcriptionally profiled during early infection of a compatible host, wheat, and a noncompatible host, Brachypodium distachyon. The study identified regulatory programs common to both hosts as well as genes with striking wheat-specific expression. Large clusters of coregulated genes and highly expressed genes on accessory chromosomes highlighted genomic organization relevant to host specialization and virulence.
title: Expression Profiling of the Wheat Pathogen Zymoseptoria tritici Reveals Genomic Patterns of Transcription and Host-Specific Regulatory Programs
author: Ronny Kellner; Amitava Bhattacharyya; Stephan Poppe; Tiffany Y. Hsu; Rachel B. Brem; Eva H. Stukenbrock
keywords: Mycosphaerella graminicola; RNA-seq; gene duplication; host adaptation; plant pathogenic fungi; supernumerary chromosomes

abstract: Transcriptomic responses to heat and cold were compared across 20 native Australian plant species from contrasting arid, alpine and temperate biomes using de novo transcriptome assemblies and 188 RNA-sequencing libraries. Conserved stress-response pathways were observed across taxa, but response magnitude differed among biomes, and transcriptomic plasticity was largely independent of photosystem II thermal-tolerance plasticity.
title: Transcriptomic Temperature Stress Responses Show Differentiation Between Biomes for Diverse Plants
author: Samuel C. Andrew; Rosalie J. Harris; Chris Coppin; Adrienne B. Nicotra; Andrea Leigh; Karel Mokany
keywords: climate change vulnerability; comparative transcriptomics; de novo transcriptomics; local adaptation; photosystem II thermal tolerance

abstract: Thermal plasticity of gene expression was studied in Drosophila simulans populations evolved in hot and cold environments. After more than 60 generations in the hot environment, 325 genes had evolved changes in plasticity relative to the ancestral population, and plasticity increased in 75% of these genes. The affected genes were enriched for functions including chitin metabolism, glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation.
title: The Evolution of Phenotypic Plasticity in Response to Temperature Stress
author: François Mallard; Viola Nolte; Christian Schlötterer
keywords: Drosophila; experimental evolution; gene expression; phenotypic plasticity; temperature adaptation

abstract: The morphological responses of Zymoseptoria tritici to environmental stresses were characterized across four strains. All tested stresses induced morphological changes, but responses differed among strains. The fungus formed chlamydospores that survived extreme cold, heat and drought better than other cell types, and transcriptomic analysis indicated co-regulation of morphogenesis and virulence-factor expression.
title: Morphological changes in response to environmental stresses in the fungal plant pathogen Zymoseptoria tritici
author: Carolina Sardinha Francisco; Xin Ma; Maria Manuela Zwyssig; Bruce A. McDonald; Javier Palma-Guerrero

abstract: Drosophila melanogaster from opposing slopes of Evolution Canyon in Israel were compared to investigate adaptation to divergent microclimates. Several hundred genes were differentially expressed and dozens of RNA-editing sites differed between slopes. Temperature influenced editing at more sites than genetic differences, and CRISPR mutagenesis validated an intronic SNP in prominin that regulates editing levels.
title: Regulation of gene expression and RNA editing in Drosophila adapting to divergent microclimates
author: Arielle L. Yablonovitch; Jeremy Fu; Kexin Li; Simpla Mahato; Lin Kang; Eugenia Rashkovetsky; Abraham B. Korol; Hua Tang; Pawel Michalak; Andrew C. Zelhof; Eviatar Nevo; Jin Billy Li

abstract: Experimental evolution was used to investigate the genetic architecture of thermal adaptation in a natural Drosophila simulans population. Transcriptome and respiration measurements revealed extensive metabolic rewiring after about 60 generations in a hot environment. Genome-wide polymorphism analysis identified two interacting selection targets, Sestrin and SNF4Aγ, implicating AMPK as a central factor in rapid thermal adaptation.
title: A simple genetic basis of adaptation to a novel thermal environment results in complex metabolic rewiring in Drosophila
author: François Mallard; Viola Nolte; Ray Tobler; Martin Kapun; Christian Schlötterer
keywords: Evolve and resequence; Experimental evolution; Pool-Seq; RNASeq; Thermal adaptation
